newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Kabila's Congo, Sierra Leone to fill OAU agenda.
newsitem.headline: Kabila's Congo, Sierra Leone to fill OAU agenda.

text.p: African leaders gathered in Zimbabwe on Monday for a three-day summit dominated by the promise of democracy for the continent's third-largest state and signs of modest economic growth after decades of decline.
Public sessions of the Organisation of African Unity summit were expected to focus on consolidation of the fledgling African economic recovery reflected in a series of positive indicators this year.

But the real work will be in behind-the-scenes meetings on the end of Mobutu Sese Seko's 32-year dictatorship in Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the troubled external relations of Libya and Nigeria.

The military coup in Sierra Leone, where Nigerian forces launched a bid on Monday to restore ousted President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, was also on the draft agenda drawn up by foreign ministers ahead of the summit.
Laurent Kabila, president of the new Congo, arrived to a personal welcome by Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe on Sunday.
Though no arrangements were in place by Monday morning, a member of his delegation said Kabila would spend much of his time in Harare in personal meetings with other African leaders.
Schoolchildren dressed in the green, yellow and red colours of Zimbabwe's flag sang and danced for guests arriving at the hotel venue.
Officials said they expected about 30 heads of state or government from the 53 member states to attend all or part of the summit.

The local Ziana news agency said the outgoing chairman, President Paul Biya of Cameroon, had cancelled at the last moment and had sent Prime Minister Peter Musonge to formally hand over the OAU reins to Mugabe, Zimbabwe's president since 1980.
Nigerian military leader General Sani Abacha and Libya's Muammar Gadaffi were among African leaders who were expected, but had not arrived by mid-morning.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan arrived aboard a South African aircraft on Sunday, mainly for a meeting on Monday with Kabila. South African President Nelson Mandela arrived on Monday and was also to meet privately with Kabila.
Mandela has criticised Western governments for questioning Kabila's commitment to human rights and democracy, saying he has been demonised before he has been given a chance to show his intentions.

But Western diplomats in Harare said Mandela, widely regarded as the moral leader of Africa, had come under pressure from the United States to moderate his support for Kabila and urge him to demonstrate a true commitment to democracy.
South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said on Monday he hoped the summit in Zimbabwe would take decisions on international help for the former Zaire.
"The task in the new Congo is so great that South Africa will not be able to help on its own," Pahad said, adding that South Africa would prefer to help as part of a world initiative.

"We would think it should be an OAU-United Nations effort because world institutions like the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, and the United Nations as a whole, would have to play a role.
"We hope that at the summit...some decisions will be taken in relation to how we can coordinate an international effort," Pahad said on South African state radio.
